title.en: No talking before davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats that the first words of the day should be before Hashem and that talking before Shacharis costs the help from Heaven, while allowing short, kind words and holy words that prepare for davening. He tells the bachurim to daven slowly, rise earlier, and daven with their yeshiva as its rules require.

title.en: The worlds of davening and the Kaddeishim

summary.en: The Mashgiach maps davening onto the worlds: korbanos in Asiyah, Pesukei d'Zimrah in Yetzirah, the brachos of Krias Shema in Beriah, and Shemoneh Esrei before the King, then the descent that brings the shefa down, with a Kaddish at each passage. He concludes that although halachah permits a latecomer to skip, by pnimiyus one should not make a habit of it.

title.en: Shabbos davening and the baal tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says coming late on Shabbos loses diamonds, since the Shabbos davening is far higher, and asks those who cannot sing well to daven quietly. A baal tefillah must lift the tzibbur and not rush, as shown by a story of the Sanzer Rav leading a hasty chazzan away from the amud.

title.en: Every day a new world, every tefillah new tikkunim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that since creation no day has had the same task, so although the words of davening repeat, their inner kavanos differ, and the words composed with ruach hakodesh effect tikkunim even unknowingly. Each morning one makes a new covenant with Hashem like Adam on his first day, each Krias Shema is a new kabbalas ol, and a lost tefillah cannot be repaired the next day.

title.en: The beginning carries the whole act

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the halachah that a sofer must say at the start that he writes for the sanctity of the Sefer Torah, and that this beginning holds even when his mind is later absorbed. He applies it to learning, bringing the Tanya on saying it each hour because of the changing combinations of the Name, to davening for the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, and to living in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Modeh Ani and the first moments of the day

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares waking to a new birth: just as the yetzer hara comes to a child before the yetzer tov, it rushes in each morning, so Modeh Ani must be said the moment one opens his eyes, which is why it contains no Name of Hashem. The first word, thought, act and sight of the day should be with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, such as looking at the tzitzis or the mezuzah.

title.en: A Jewish name and its shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that each Jew is sent with his own shlichus, alluded to in his name, bringing Yaakov's question to the angel and Rashi's comment, and suggests combining the letters of one's name with the Name Havayah on waking. He warns against being called by a non-Jewish name, telling of a heretic named Eliezer whose name helped him do teshuvah, and closes by recalling the yahrzeit of Reb Yankele of Pshevorsk.

catalogTitle: ”כי קרוב אליך הדבר וכו'” למה כל כך קשה לקיים תורה ומצות? והתירוץ - “עצבות.” עצות להיות בשמחה. כל יסורים באים מב' אותיות ראשונות שבשם הוי'.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on the end of Tanya chapter 25, how a Jew's readiness to give his life rather than worship idols makes every mitzvah 'very near', and why both the aveirah and the union of a mitzvah are eternal, while teshuvah restores the bond.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that all positive mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi Hashem' and all prohibitions out of 'Lo yihyeh lecha', so every aveirah cuts a Jew off from Hashem as idolatry would. Since every Jew is ready to give his life against avodah zarah, he can tell himself, facing a temptation, that the far smaller sacrifice of giving up a desire is surely within reach; this is how 'ki karov eilecha hadavar' is fulfilled. Even a 'temporary' aveirah is not temporary, since above time everything is eternal. He explains bittul and 'Hashem Echad', the world as a mirage of hester panim, and that the union of a mitzvah, like the Torah, is eternal, while teshuvah undoes the cutting off. He admits the idea is hard for minds molded by this world. He then discusses why Selach Lanu is said three times a day, why the Tanya speaks of positive mitzvos, achta v'ashuv, why Moshe taught 'b'chol nafshecha' before Eretz Yisrael, and answers a question on teshuvah and forgiveness.

en: All positive mitzvos are branches of 'Anochi Hashem' and all prohibitions of 'Lo yihyeh lecha', so any aveirah detaches a Jew from Hashem as idolatry does.

Since a Jew is ready to give his life rather than worship idols, he can reason that giving up a smaller desire, a lesser 'mesiras nefesh', is surely within his power; this makes serving Hashem 'very near'.
Above, Hashem and His will are beyond time, so an aveirah 'just for now' is registered forever, and so is the union of a mitzvah and the Torah itself.
An aveirah cuts a person off eternally, but teshuvah removes the cutting off and he is again eternally attached.
Selach Lanu is repeated three times a day because there is most likely bittul Torah in between, and because a person who grows needs new forgiveness for what he did before.
Moshe Rabbeinu taught 'b'chol nafshecha' to the Jews entering Eretz Yisrael so they could use the reckoning of mesiras nefesh against every other temptation there.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh makes every mitzvah near

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that every mitzvah is a branch of the first two commandments, so every aveirah detaches a Jew from Hashem. Since every Jew stands ready to die rather than worship idols, he can tell himself that giving up a smaller desire is surely within reach; this is how 'ki karov eilecha hadavar' is fulfilled.

title.en: No such thing as a temporary aveirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's point that a Jew must give his life even for idolatry 'only for now', after which he would do teshuvah. Above, past, present and future are one, so an aveirah, and also refraining from one, is registered as eternal.

title.en: Bittul and Hashem Echad

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the purpose of avodas Hashem is to be nullified to Hashem: 'Echad' means there is nothing but Him, and the world that seems to exist on its own is a mirage, hester panim. One who gives up his desires to cleave to Hashem merits gilui panim and feels it in his soul.

title.en: The eternal union and the eternal Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the union formed when a person withstands a desire is eternal, because Hashem and His will, expressed in the Torah, are above time and never change. An aveirah cuts a person off eternally, but teshuvah restores the bond; he answers a listener's question and compares the Torah's changing appearance to a cloud.

title.en: Accepting a hard idea with emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach admits that this half page is hard to grasp, not because the logic is weak but because minds molded by this world take it as the world of truth. He says one must accept it with emunah, as one moves on past a difficult Tosafos, and warns that the next chapter will be similar.

title.en: Why Selach Lanu three times a day

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Selach Lanu is said three times a day if Hashem surely forgives the first time. He answers with the Tanya that even a masmid interrupts his learning in between, so new bittul Torah needs new forgiveness, and a deep teshuvah need not be repeated.

title.en: Growing teshuvah, stains, and achta v'ashuv

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that one who grows is held to account again for old aveiros, and Yom Kippur brings teshuvah from a higher root. He explains that the Tanya speaks of positive mitzvos because prohibitions leave a stain needing more, with parables of a stained shirt and a broken bottle of wine. A person who knows he will likely fall again is not 'achta v'ashuv'.

title.en: B'chol nafshecha before Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Moshe Rabbeinu commanded 'b'chol nafshecha' in Krias Shema to Jews about to enter Eretz Yisrael, where they were promised victory and faced no forced idolatry. He answers that it was an eitzah: the reckoning of readiness for mesiras nefesh would help them withstand every other temptation there.

title.en: Teshuvah first, then forgiveness

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Mashgiach explains that teshuvah comes first and the request for forgiveness after it, so the bracha is made knowing it is accepted. He mentions vidui in Tachanun for individual sins and one collective sin, and says that unlike other requests, forgiveness is guaranteed.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jewish emunah rests on the revelation at Har Sinai, witnessed by an entire nation and handed down unchanged, and that the nations' denial of it and their hatred of the Jews come from jealousy of the chosen people, as with Yosef's brothers.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mesirus nefesh of whole Jewish communities, which goes beyond the trained loyalty of a gentile soldier: Jews carry emunah in the heart. Unlike other faiths, each founded by one individual, Jews believe what an entire nation saw at Har Sinai. Through Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem', he shows that millions witnessed the revelation, comparing it to undeniable history such as George Washington or Julius Caesar. Every Jew became a prophet, the Sefer Torah was written before eyewitnesses, and every copy is identical. Following the Rambam, belief in Moshe rests on Sinai, so the first mitzvah he taught begins the Torah; and the Torah is eternal, so a prophet who changes it is false. Small differences arose in galus and between the tribes' middos, yet the foundations are shared. The nations deny this from jealousy of the chosen people, as Yosef's brothers did.

en: Jews, even whole cities and communities, gave their lives rather than convert, because emunah is in their heart and not only taught and drilled into them.
Other religions were begun by a single person, while the Jewish faith rests on what a whole nation received at Har Sinai.
An event seen by millions and passed on by a whole people cannot be falsified, just as no one can deny George Washington or Julius Caesar.
Following the Rambam, Jews believe Moshe Rabbeinu because they themselves heard at Sinai Hashem appoint him to teach them the Torah.
The Torah is eternal; no prophet may add to it or take from it, and one who claims Hashem changed a mitzvah is a false prophet.
The foundations of the Torah are the same among all Jews; only small details differ, through forgetting in galus or the tribes' different middos.
The nations hate the Jews out of jealousy, because deep down they know the Jews are the chosen people, as Yosef's brothers were jealous of him.

title.en: Jewish mesirus nefesh for emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts a gentile soldier, trained from childhood to die for his country, with Jews who gave their lives rather than convert, even whole communities during the Crusades. He explains that Jews have emunah in the heart, an inheritance from the Avos.

title.en: Faiths founded by one man

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every other faith was started by one individual: the founder of Christianity, who made religion easy by permitting forbidden things, and Muhammad, who claimed G-d had changed the Torah. Jews, he says, do not believe one man but what a whole nation received.

title.en: Rashi's question and a nation at Sinai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem', and starts building the answer: millions stood at Har Sinai, heard Hashem and became prophets. A whole people cannot pass on a lie to its children, just as no one can deny George Washington, Julius Caesar or Alexander the Great.

title.en: The Sefer Torah written before witnesses

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew at Sinai was a prophet, and at the end of forty years Moshe wrote the Sefer Torah before people who had seen everything in it; every Jew wrote his own, so all are identical to this day. He brings 'panim b'fanim' and 'ki sh'al na', and notes that Christians and Muslims admit Matan Torah but claim Hashem changed His mind.

title.en: Why we believe Moshe Rabbeinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah: Jews believe Moshe because at Sinai they heard Hashem appoint him to teach them the rest of the Torah, after they asked that Moshe speak to them. Therefore, he concludes, the Torah should have begun with 'Hachodesh', the first mitzvah Moshe taught, which answers Rashi's question.

title.en: The Torah is eternal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that the Torah stands forever, with the pesukim against adding or subtracting, 'the revealed things are ours forever' and 'it is not in heaven'. A prophet cannot change a halachah, so one who says a mitzvah was only for a time, like moving Shabbos to Sunday or Friday, is a false prophet.

title.en: One Torah, small differences

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the same Torah passed down through the generations; in galus some details were forgotten and disputes arose, but the foundations are shared by all Jews. Disputes are 'eilu v'eilu': middas chesed and middas din both come from Hashem, each tribe had its own judges, as with Beis Hillel and Beis Shammai, and the tefillin of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam.

title.en: Why the nations deny and hate

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the nations, who admit Matan Torah, claim it was changed, and why they hate Jews even today when neither they nor many Jews keep their religion. He answers that they cannot bear that the Jews are the chosen people, and brings this week's sedra: Yosef's brothers saw their father loved him more and hated him from jealousy.

title.en: Announcements and mazel tov

summary.en: After the shiur there are announcements about a minyan for those who have not yet davened Maariv, and mazel tov wishes to a chassan.

oneLiner.en: Through stories of tzaddikim, the Mashgiach shows the bachurim how great people went out of their way never to trouble or pain another Jew, even at a cost to themselves or to a mitzvah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach tells the bachurim that this time he wants to speak about middos, and to do it through stories of tzaddikim. He tells how Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld asked each Yom Tov visitor whether he had been at the Kosel, so that a guest sitting with him would not feel slighted, and how he moved back to the Old City before his passing so that the Jews at his levayah would not have to walk far. He gave the Rosh Hashanah musaf to the son of the late chazzan for the widow's sake. The Chofetz Chaim skipped the na'anuim on the town's only esrog so as not to pain those who had none. Rav Moshe Kliers declared a broken eruv kosher to protect the honor of the Sefardi chacham, and Rav Chaim Ozer weighed a servant's trouble and kept a guest company in the sukkah. After taking leave of the bachurim for several weeks, the Mashgiach ends with the Chofetz Chaim's rebuke of talmidim who laughed at a broken-hearted woman, and Rav Elchonon Wasserman's seriousness.

en: The Mashgiach says he is speaking to the bachurim about middos this time, through stories of how tzaddikim served Hashem.
Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld returned to the Old City before his passing against his doctors' advice, so that Jews would not have to walk far to his burial on Har HaZeisim.
Rav Yosef Chaim had the son of the late baal musaf lead musaf on Rosh Hashanah, so that the widow would not suffer hearing a stranger in her husband's place.
The Chofetz Chaim did not shake the only esrog in town during Hallel, so as not to cause pain to everyone who could not do so.
Rav Moshe Kliers explained that he called a broken eruv kosher because the honor of the Torah, embodied in the Sefardi chacham, outweighed an issur derabbanan.

Rav Chaim Ozer considered the trouble of his household servant before taking a summer apartment, and, though exempt from sukkah, came down to keep a poor guest company because he was not exempt from hachnasas orchim.
The Chofetz Chaim sharply rebuked talmidim who laughed at a simple woman's words, saying one may not laugh at a person with a heavy heart.

title.en: Middos through stories; the visitors and the Kosel

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he will speak about middos through stories of tzaddikim. He tells how Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld asked each Yom Tov visitor whether he had been at the Kosel, so that the Lubliner Rav sitting with him would not feel slighted.

title.en: Returning to the Old City before his passing

summary.en: Rav Yosef Chaim, sent by his doctors to the airier New City, moved back to the crowded Old City a few weeks before his passing. He explained that his burial would be on Har HaZeisim, and he did not want everyone to walk a long way from the New City.

title.en: The mourner who led musaf on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: When the baal musaf died days before Rosh Hashanah, Rav Yosef Chaim delayed the choice and then sent the deceased's son to the amud. Asked about the Shulchan Aruch's rule on a mourner leading the davening, he said the widow in the ezras nashim would otherwise suffer, and the Mashgiach calls this the thinking of a tzaddik.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's esrog without na'anuim

summary.en: During the First World War there was one esrog in Radin, brought for the Chofetz Chaim, and everyone made the brachah on it. At Hallel he did not shake it, explaining that the others could fulfil the mitzvah of taking it but could not do na'anuim, and he would not cause them pain.

title.en: The eruv in Teveria and the chacham's honor

summary.en: In Teveria the Sefardi chacham oversaw the eruv. When it broke on Shabbos, Rav Moshe Kliers declared it kosher; after Shabbos the Gemara showed it was pasul. Asked privately, he explained that announcing it would have shamed the chacham and the honor of the Torah, which outweighs an issur derabbanan.

title.en: Rav Chaim Ozer: the servant and the guest in the sukkah

summary.en: Rav Chaim Ozer hesitated to take a spacious summer apartment until the servant agreed, since its kitchen was far from the dining room. Later, ill and exempt from sukkah, he sent a poor guest to eat in the sukkah and came down to sit with him, citing Avraham Avinu's hachnasas orchim.

title.en: Taking leave of the bachurim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bachurim that his doctors are urging him to spend several weeks in Miami for his health, so they will not meet for about four weeks. He says he will miss the davening here and asks that he return with better health.

title.en: Not laughing at a heavy heart

summary.en: A simple woman told the Chofetz Chaim she could not pray at her parents' graves because they were alive; the talmidim laughed and he rebuked them sharply. The Mashgiach adds that Rav Elchonon Wasserman, following Chazal on laughter in this world, was never seen smiling except once, and closes with a l'chaim.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Mashgiach speaks of the preciousness of Eretz Yisroel and warns that one who lives there must keep renewing his appreciation and be truly planted in the land through Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with a Jew who comes from outside the land and merits to live in Eretz Yisroel, the good land the Torah praises as a land of streams of water. The danger, he says, is that one grows used to it, so a person needs constant renewal and must work for it. One indirect way is through davening: when a person concentrates in Pesukei d'Zimra on the praises of Yerushalayim, and on the blessing for Yerushalayim in Shemoneh Esrei. A Jew in Boro Park says these words, but feels far away; a Jew in the land feels close, and must thank Hashem. Citing the week's sedra about settling the land, the Mashgiach says one must rejoice in Eretz Yisroel. He then compares a log laid on the ground, which only rots, to a planted tree that grows: being in the land is not enough, one must be planted in it with the Torah of Eretz Yisroel.

en: A person living in Eretz Yisroel can grow used to it, so he needs constant renewal and must work for it.
One indirect way to renew this feeling is through davening, by concentrating on the praises of Yerushalayim in Pesukei d'Zimra and in Shemoneh Esrei.
A Jew abroad says the same words about Yerushalayim but feels far, while one in the land feels close and must thank Hashem.
Being in Eretz Yisroel is not enough; like a planted tree rather than a log on the ground, one must be planted there through Torah.

candidateTopics: being rooted in the land through Torah

title.en: The preciousness of Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of a Jew who merits to live in Eretz Yisroel, warns against growing used to it, and suggests renewing the feeling through the praises of Yerushalayim in davening. He ends with the parable of a log versus a planted tree: one must be rooted in the land through Torah.

catalogTitle: אגרת "להשכילך בינה" - בענין בני חיי מזוני כתוב - “בטל רצונך מפני רצונו.” יש צער אחד שהוא אמת וזה צער שעבר רצון ה'. ומכל מקום - אל תעסוק בו הרבה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach learns Tanya chapter 26: the yetzer hara can only be overpowered with the alertness that comes from simcha, the only true sadness is remorse over aveiros at set times, and worldly suffering is relieved by knowing it comes from the hidden world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews how chapter 25 made serving Hashem seem easy, then turns to chapter 26: like a wrestler, or an ox against a lion, the lazy side loses, so the yetzer hara can only be overcome with alertness born of simcha, while sadness itself breeds craving. Sadness has an advantage only when it is remorse over aveiros, and only for its product, teshuvah and the joy of reconciliation, felt at set times such as Tikkun Chatzos, which the Mashgiach explains at length. Sadness over livelihood or other worldly matters, by the Tanya's standard, is nothing. The remedy is to know that hardships come from the hidden world, too high for this world to bear, and to accept them with simcha, as the stories of the Ger Tzedek Graf Potocki and of the Alter Rebbe's arrest show. The Mashgiach admits this level is very hard for our generation.

en: Like a wrestler who loses when he is lazy and heavy even if he is stronger, a person can only overpower the yetzer hara with alertness that comes from simcha and an open heart.
Sadness itself feeds the yetzer hara, because an unhappy person seeks gratification elsewhere.
The only true sadness is remorse over aveiros, and its value lies only in what it produces: teshuvah and the simcha that follows it.
Even this remorse belongs only to set times, such as before sleep or Rosh Hashanah, and not all day.
Sadness over children, health or livelihood has no place by the Tanya's standard, since Hashem's hashgachah pratis puts a person where it is best for him.
Hardships come from the hidden world, which is higher than the revealed one; one who accepts them with simcha will see them transformed into revealed kindness.

title.en: Is it a cinch? The wrestler and the lion

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews chapter 25, that every aveirah separates a person from Hashem like avodah zarah, which seems to make being a tzaddik easy. He then opens chapter 26 with the wrestling analogy: a stronger fighter who is lazy and heavy loses, as an ox loses to a lion.

title.en: Overpowering the yetzer hara with simcha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that laziness comes from sadness and a stone-like heart, while alertness comes from simcha in knowing one has a Provider in heaven. He shows how sadness itself drives a person to seek gratification, and says the Tanya's demand for a heart free of worry applies, to our degree, even in our generation.

title.en: The one true sadness: remorse over aveiros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the passuk that every sorrow has an advantage: not that sadness is good, but that remorse over aveiros leads to teshuvah and the simcha of reconciliation, like two friends who make up. This sadness belongs only at set times, and he reads it into the pesukim of Tehillim 51 about a broken spirit leading to joy.

title.en: Tikkun Chatzos and the seudah of Dovid HaMelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Tikkun Chatzos, Dovid HaMelech's midnight tefillah, and parallels the tefillos of the Avos and of Dovid to the Shabbos seudos and Melaveh Malkah. Tehillim 51 is part of Tikkun Chatzos, where a person laments the churban and, more deeply, his own inner Beis HaMikdash ruined by his aveiros, and then rises to simcha.

title.en: Light after darkness; worldly sadness is nothing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that joy after sadness is like light after darkness, and brings the curse for not serving Hashem with simcha. By the Tanya's standard, sadness over income or other worldly matters is a child's complaint over a broken house of blocks; he asks whether a person is sad over his aveiros or over his income, and admits this chapter demands more than we can offer.

title.en: Bnei, chayei, mezonei and the hidden world

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a person can free himself from sadness over children, life and sustenance, and brings Chazal that one must bless and accept the bad with simcha as the good. He explains the two halves of the Shem Havayah, the hidden world and the revealed world: hardships come from the higher, hidden world, which this world cannot bear, and they bring a person closer to Hashem.

title.en: Those who rejoice in suffering

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that accepting hardship with simcha turns the hidden into revealed kindness, and that a person should say even of undesirable things that they are for the good. He brings the Gemara about those who accept suffering with love, and the passuk that those who love Hashem are like the sun going out in its strength: the tzaddik feels the pressure like a tight shoe but disregards it in his joy of closeness to Hashem.

title.en: The Ger Tzedek and the house of blocks

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells briefly of Graf Potocki, a great Polish lord who became a Jew and was condemned to be burned. When the executioner asked whether he would take revenge, he answered with a parable of children's houses of blocks: this world is worth nothing to him, and he is going to a better world.

title.en: The sun drawn from its sheath

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that for such tzaddikim all suffering is suffering of love, and that the spiritual sun will be uncovered from its sheath, so the hidden world will shine in this world on those who take refuge in Hashem's shadow. He sums up the Tanya's remedy: realize that worldly hardships are nothing and be happy with Hashem who is hidden in them.

title.en: Reb Shmuel Munkes and the Alter Rebbe's arrest

summary.en: The Mashgiach admits this level is not for everybody, then tells how Reb Shmuel Munkes told the Alter Rebbe not to hide from arrest: if he is a Rebbe he need fear nothing, and if not, by what right did he take away thousands of Jews' appreciation of this world. He concludes that this paragraph may not be for our generation, and that other aids to simcha must be found.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan and Pesach are the time of renewal and the 'point' of beginning, the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu and of emunah, and that the matzah is filled with holy Names of emunah and redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaChodesh: Nissan is the month of renewal, when the Jewish people became a nation and, according to the halachah, the world was created. Nature itself comes back to life in Nissan; the birds return and fill the air with song, and he explains why morning is called tzafra and night ramsha. Among the three Regalim, Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, yet only Pesach carries kares, because Pesach is the 'point', the beginning and the bond with Hashem, like Avraham Avinu, after whom the first blessing is named Magen Avraham. Pesach is the time to daven and say Hallel with freshness, and a kind of techiyas hamesim. It is the Yom Tov of emunah: matzah is the 'food of faith', filled with holy Names of emunah and geulah. He closes with the gematria of lechem and matzah and a call to keep Pesach with kedushah and care.

en: Nissan is the time of renewal: the Jewish people became a nation then, and the world itself was created in Nissan.
Shavuos and Sukkos are higher Yamim Tovim than Pesach, but Pesach is the 'point' and the beginning, the bond with Hashem, which is why only Pesach carries kares.
Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, and the time of emunah, the point in a Jew's heart on which all mitzvos rest.
On Pesach one must be fresh: daven, say Hallel and the Haggadah with freshness and joy, and rise as in a techiyas hamesim.
The essence of the matzah is the holy Names within it, Names of emunah and of geulah; the baked matzah is only their envelope.

title.en: Nissan, the month of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaChodesh and explains that in Nissan the Jewish people became a nation. He brings the dispute whether the world was created in Nissan or Tishrei, Tosafos' resolution, and that the Avos were born in Nissan, so Nissan is the time for a Jew to renew himself.

title.en: Nature comes back to life

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the dead winter fields and trees revive in Nissan and the birds return and sing. He explains why morning is called tzafra and night ramsha, says a Jew sings to Hashem at all times, and brings Shir HaShirim on the passing of the winter.

title.en: Pesach, the point of beginning

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the three Regalim: Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, as seen from Hallel, yet Pesach is the beginning, like Avraham among the Avos. Only Pesach carries kares, the opposite of the bond with Hashem that Pesach makes, and this is why the blessing is Magen Avraham; emunah is the point on which all mitzvos rest.

title.en: Milah, korban Pesach and Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the only two positive mitzvos with kares, milah and the korban Pesach, are both tied to Avraham Avinu, and that Avraham's great events happened on Pesach. Pesach is the bond with Hashem, like a chuppah, while the other Yamim Tovim hold higher things.

title.en: Freshness and techiyas hamesim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says on Pesach one must daven, say Hallel and the Haggadah freshly, bringing the passuk in Eichah and the Targum that the 'mo'ed' there is Pesach. The revival of nature is a techiyas hamesim; he brings the haftorah of Yechezkel's dry bones and says every Jew must rise anew on Pesach.

title.en: Everything is new on Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the whole Yom Tov is built on renewal: new clothes, a painted house, dishes not seen for twelve months. Pesach is the time of emunah, and he brings the Yismach Yisrael that at the seder one plants emunah in the children by telling them of yetzias Mitzrayim.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the mitzvah of emunah to Avraham, the first believer, and discusses the nusach 'Ha lachma anya' versus 'Kehah lachma anya'. He brings the Zohar that matzah is the food of faith, as the Jews left Egypt with only matzah, and says the matzah is full of holy Names.

title.en: The holy Names inside the matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Divrei Chaim after the seder and gives the mashal of an esrog that is a plain citrus fruit all year and a holy object on Sukkos. So too the essence of the matzah is the Names of geulah within it, the same as in Egypt; he then tells the bachurim to help at home, learn hilchos Pesach and burn their chametz.

title.en: Lechem and matzah in gematria

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that lechem equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times that Name spelled out in full, a higher level of holy Names. He closes with a warning to keep Pesach with care and kedushah, since Pesach is emunah, the most important thing a Jew has.

oneLiner.en: Before starting to learn Tanya with the bachurim, the Mashgiach traces how the secrets of the Torah came down to the Ba'al Shem Tov's way of avodah, explains what makes the Tanya and its author unique, and tells stories of the Ba'al HaTanya's imprisonment.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the four levels of Torah given at Sinai, pshat, remez, drush and sod, and explains that the secrets were passed only to the greatest students, until Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote the Zohar and the Arizal revealed more. The Ba'al Shem Tov taught how to use these secrets for avodas Hashem, and the Maggid's students wrote sefarim on the weekly sedra. The Tanya is different: it builds its subject in order, chapter after chapter, so it opens the other chassidic sefarim. He brings the Satmar Rav's advice to learn Tanya in order to come to want to serve Hashem, describes the Ba'al HaTanya's lofty soul and his Shulchan Aruch, in which every word is weighed, and tells stories of his arrest and interrogation. He closes by announcing that the Tanya shiur will begin next Tuesday.

en: The secrets of the Torah were given at Sinai but passed only to the greatest students, until the Zohar and the Arizal's writings put them in sefarim.
The Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching is to use the secrets of the Torah for avodas Hashem, and his students' sefarim show how.
Unlike the other sefarim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students, which follow the sedra, the Tanya builds its subject in order, each chapter continuing the one before.
The Tanya teaches how to serve Hashem and is also the key to understanding the other chassidic sefarim, such as the Meor Einayim and the Kedushas Levi.
In the Ba'al HaTanya's works, the Tanya and his Shulchan Aruch, every word and even every letter is measured and weighed.

title.en: The secrets of the Torah and their transmission

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah was given with four levels, pardes, and that its secrets were handed down only to the greatest students. After the Churban, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote the Zohar, and later the Arizal revealed new secrets with permission from Heaven.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and his students' sefarim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the Ba'al Shem Tov took the secrets of the Zohar and the Arizal and used them for avodas Hashem, and lists the sefarim of the Maggid and his students. He explains that most tzaddikim did not write their own teachings, and tells how the Meor Einayim let only the teachings he did not remember be written down.

title.en: Why the Tanya is different

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya, unlike the other chassidic sefarim, is a structured work that builds chapter by chapter. He notes that some Rebbes held it reveals too much, but brings the Bnei Yissaschar, the Satmar Rav's advice to learn Tanya in order to want to serve Hashem, and Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learning it in Torah Vodaath.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya and his Shulchan Aruch

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya opens up the other chassidic sefarim, describes the Ba'al HaTanya as a soul from the world of Atzilus and a great chacham, and tells how the Maggid had him write a Shulchan Aruch, telling him to rewrite its first chapters simply, without sodos.

title.en: Every word weighed: the Shulchan Aruch HaRav

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Ba'al HaTanya deliberating for weeks over one vav in the Tanya, explains why chassidim call him 'the Mashgiach', and brings Reb Yaakov Kamenetsky and Reb Meir Arik on the weight of the Shulchan Aruch HaRav. He adds that it is one of the best ways to understand the Gemara.

title.en: Stories of the Ba'al HaTanya's arrest

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Czar arrested the Ba'al HaTanya, visited him in disguise and tested his wisdom, how he avoided a hidden pit on the way to the judge, and how he had the boat stopped for kiddush levanah by natural means. He ends with the judge's last question about the Tanya, which the Ba'al HaTanya answered only with a smile.

title.en: Starting to learn Tanya together

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces that he will learn Tanya with the bachurim, as he did several times in Torah Vodaath with their fathers, the founders of Emunas Yisroel, who gained much from it. He says it will go slowly and open new understanding of Torah and avodas Hashem, recalls the Ba'al Shem Tov's words about Moshiach, and sets the start for next Tuesday.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Mashgiach teaches that whoever defeats the 'snake' of the yetzer hara receives the 'king's daughter' of tefillah, and that the unprecedented tests of this generation signal how great the reward will be.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach brings the saying that whoever kills the snake is given the king's daughter, and explains that the snake is the yetzer hara and the king's daughter is tefillah. One who overcomes the yetzer hara merits real tefillah, which not everyone merits; it needs preparation. He then says that the tests of today are enormous: with all the new devices and tools that keep coming, this generation faces tests that earlier generations never had. Still, one must work hard against the yetzer hara, not give in, and ask Hashem for help. The very size of these tests, he says, is a sign that what will be received is very great. He mentions a new form of Torah, its inner dimension, that is being revealed, and says one must rejoice, since the tests can be fought and Hashem will help.

en: Whoever kills the 'snake' receives the 'king's daughter': the snake is the yetzer hara and the king's daughter is tefillah.
Not everyone merits true tefillah; it requires preparation.
The tests of this generation, brought by the many new devices, are enormous and were never faced by earlier generations.
One must work hard against the yetzer hara, not give in, and ask Hashem for help.

candidateTopics: the snake and the king's daughter

title.en: The snake, the king's daughter and today's tests

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the saying about killing the snake and receiving the king's daughter as overcoming the yetzer hara to merit tefillah. He describes the unprecedented tests brought by today's new devices, says their size signals a great reward, and urges rejoicing and asking Hashem for help.

catalogTitle: Shabbos - A Day That Sings For Itself (Intro.to the תפילות of שבת)

oneLiner.en: Introducing the tefillos of Shabbos, the Mashgiach explains that tefillah is the service of the heart that connects us to the Avos, and that Shabbos, the seventh, is the day that sings for itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah to serve Hashem with the heart, which Chazal call tefillah. The Avos instituted the three tefillos, the karbanos correspond to them, and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah composed the nusach; the first bracha connects us to the Avos. He brings the machlokes of the Rambam and the Ramban on the daily mitzvah of tefillah, and stresses that tefillah requires kavanah, knowing the words and putting one's heart into them. Tefillah has endless depths, and the Arizal writes that each tefillah until Moshiach is different. He discusses davening without kavanah, especially in the first bracha. Learning Sefer Bereishis likewise connects us to the Avos. Shabbos, the day of avodas Hashem, drops the twelve weekday brachos that parallel the shevatim and reaches back to the Avos. Kabbalas Shabbos culminates in Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos: Shabbos sings for itself, as the seventh note completes the harp of creation.

en: Tefillah is the avodah of the heart; a tefillah said without the heart, the Mashgiach says, is not called tefillah.
The first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei connects us to the Avos, who instituted tefillah, and this is the introduction to all of tefillah.
The nusach of tefillah was composed by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah with ruach hakodesh, and its depths are endless, like pshat, drush and remez in Torah.
On Shabbos the twelve middle brachos, which parallel the twelve shevatim and deal with bodily needs, are replaced by one bracha asking only for spiritual closeness, going back to the Avos.
Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos is unlike the songs of the other days: on the other days someone sang for the day, but Shabbos sings for itself.
Creation was made with seven notes, one for each day, and only on Shabbos was the harp complete, so Shabbos is the day of song.

candidateTopics: tefillah as service of the heart
Shabbos as the day of song

title.en: Tefillah, the avodah of the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah to serve Hashem with all one's heart, which Chazal call tefillah. He explains that the Avos instituted the three tefillos, that the karbanos correspond to them, and that the first bracha connects us to the Avos; a tefillah without the heart is not called tefillah.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban; the heart of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the machlokes whether there is a daily mitzvah of tefillah or only in a time of trouble, and notes that today the whole world is in trouble. He explains that the nusach was composed by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, who were prophets, and that davening with kavanah means meeting their heart with ours.

title.en: The endless depth of tefillah, and davening without kavanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the levels of kavanah in tefillah to pshat, drush and remez in Torah, and brings the Arizal that every tefillah until Moshiach is different. He then discusses one who davens without kavanah, and why today one does not repeat even the first bracha, the bracha of the Avos.

title.en: Sefer Bereishis, Shabbos and the shevatim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Sefer Bereishis, like the first bracha, connects us to the Avos. He explains that on Shabbos, the day of avodas Hashem, the twelve middle brachos for bodily needs, which parallel the twelve shevatim, are dropped for one bracha of spiritual requests, going straight to the Avos, and compares this to Yerushalayim.

title.en: Kabbalas Shabbos and the song of the seventh

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Kabbalas Shabbos: six kapitlach for the six weekdays and then Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos for the seventh, with which Shabbos is accepted. He brings Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer on the pattern of six and a seventh, and explains that unlike the Levi'im's songs of the other days, Shabbos sings for itself.

title.en: The seven-stringed harp: Shabbos, the day of song

summary.en: From the Gemara's harp of seven strings and the seven notes of music, the Mashgiach explains that creation's seven days are seven notes, complete only on Shabbos. He connects this to the seven kolos of Havu LaHashem, to Eretz Yisrael, the Kinneres and David HaMelech as the singing sevenths, and to the added mizmorim of Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: Opening a new series for bachurim on tefillah, the Mashgiach explains why he speaks so much about prayer, tells how his beis medrash grew out of a group of bachurim who wanted to daven properly, and shows that the heart of tefillah is kavanah, the awareness of standing before the King.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach announces a new series on tefillah and explains why he speaks about prayer more than Torah: the bachurim hear about Torah all week in yeshiva, while tefillah, as the Gemara says, stands at the heights of the world yet people belittle it. He tells how a group of bachurim he led in a summer camp's masmidim division learned to daven slowly, then asked for a year-round minyan; despite mockery it grew into his beis medrash, whose foundation is tefillah. He brings the Gemara's dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and the Rambam's ruling. He then teaches that tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, that the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah fixed three daily tefillos, corresponding to the Avos or the korbanos, and that as thought can disqualify a korban, thought and kavanah are the core of tefillah. He closes on the first berachah, standing before the King, and kiddush levanah.

en: The Mashgiach speaks constantly about tefillah because yeshivos speak about Torah all week, while tefillah, though it stands at the heights of the world, is belittled by people.
His beis medrash was built only because bachurim who learned well also wanted to daven well, so its foundation is tefillah.
Tefillah fulfills the mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart, and therefore its core is the heart and the thought.
The Anshei Knesses Hagedolah fixed three daily tefillos, corresponding either to the Avos or to the korbanos.
Since thought alone can invalidate a korban, and tefillah corresponds to the korbanos, thought and kavanah are the essence of tefillah.
Everything before Shemoneh Esrei is preparation, so that a person can stand in prayer feeling that he stands before the King.

title.en: Why the Mashgiach speaks about tefillah

summary.en: After a short announcement about a new commentary on Pirkei Avos, the Mashgiach opens a new series on tefillah. He recalls the Satmar Rav's drashos, explains that bachurim hear about Torah all week, and brings the Gemara that tefillah stands at the heights of the world yet people belittle it.

title.en: How the chaburah and beis medrash began

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how, at the Skverer Rebbe's instruction, he became head of the masmidim in a summer camp, taught the bachurim to daven slowly, and how their request for a year-round minyan grew, despite mockery, into a beis medrash that expanded from place to place.

title.en: A beis medrash founded on tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the beis medrash today and why the early years' davening was better, then explains that it was built for tefillah. He brings the Gemara's dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and the Rambam's ruling, and announces the new series on tefillah.

title.en: Service of the heart and the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart and shows where it appears in kriyas shema. He then describes the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah, who, when prophecy ended in the second Beis Hamikdash, strengthened Yiddishkeit with the rabbinic takanos.

title.en: Three tefillos and the power of thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the two views on whether the three tefillos correspond to the Avos or to the korbanos, and argues that since thought can invalidate a korban, thought is the core of tefillah. Without kavanah one fulfills only the rabbinic obligation, and one must ask Hashem for the kavanah itself.

title.en: Standing before the King; kiddush levanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses kavanah in the first berachah and why the Acharonim say not to repeat Shemoneh Esrei, asks why kavanah should not be needed in all the berachos, and explains that the whole tefillah prepares one to feel he stands before the King. He ends on kiddush levanah as greeting the Shechinah.

oneLiner.en: Opening the Tanya for bachurim, the Mashgiach explains why the sefer begins with the word 'Tanya', what the oath 'be a tzaddik and not a rasha' means and why it gives strength, and how the Raya Mehemna reads the four types of people in the Gemara.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins the Tanya with the Gemara in Niddah that a soul is sworn before birth to be a tzaddik and not a rasha. He brings the Chabad tradition that the opening word 'Tanya' breaks a kelipah of that name, and that the introduction addresses every Jew in every generation. Citing the Satmar Rebbe, he calls Tanya the sefer for one who wants to want to be good, and reads its letters as the future-tense prefixes. He describes the sefer's order: questions, knowledge, then avodah. He derives shevuah from sheva, the seven forces of creation, so the oath strengthens a person against the yetzer hara, as with Eliezer, and reads 'mashbi'in' as 'mashpi'in'. He then raises the Tanya's question about seeing oneself as a rasha, brings the Gemara's four types with the Raya Mehemna's reading, and ends with beinonim, Rabbah and Iyov.

en: Before a soul comes down it is sworn to be a tzaddik and not a rasha, and even if the whole world calls it a tzaddik it should be in its own eyes like a rasha.
The Tanya is a sefer in avodas Hashem for someone who wants to become better, and the Mashgiach says it answers every question one can ask in avodas Hashem.
The Tanya is built in order: questions in the first chapter, then about ten or fifteen chapters of knowledge, and only then guidance in avodah, which can be understood only with that knowledge.
An oath carries the power of all seven forces of creation and so strengthens a person against the yetzer hara.
According to the Raya Mehemna, a 'tzaddik who has bad' is a tzaddik whose evil is subordinate to him, and a 'rasha who has good' is one who has a yetzer tov but does not obey it.

title.en: Why the sefer opens with 'Tanya'

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the beraisa in Niddah the Ba'al HaTanya quotes does not begin with 'Tanya', and brings the Chabad tradition that he added the word to break a kelipah of that name. He adds that what he will say comes from sefarim or from what he heard from his rebbe, Reb Feivel Mendlowitz.

title.en: A sefer for one who wants to become better

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the introduction addresses every Jew in every generation who learns the sefer, brings the Satmar Rebbe's answer that one who wants to want should learn Tanya, and says the sefer answers every question in avodas Hashem. He then reads the four letters of 'Tanya' as the prefixes of the future tense.

title.en: The oath and the order of the Tanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the oath the soul takes, to be a tzaddik and not a rasha and to be like a rasha in its own eyes, and describes the Tanya's system: questions, then knowledge, then avodah. He says he will learn the first chapter with its questions closely and may summarize some later chapters.

title.en: Shevuah, sheva and shefa

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that shevuah comes from sheva: an oath binds a person with all seven forces of creation, which is why one may swear to strengthen himself against the yetzer hara, as Avraham made Eliezer swear. He then reads 'mashbi'in' as 'mashpi'in', since pei and beis interchange and a pei in ksav ashuri holds a hidden beis.

title.en: How can one consider himself a rasha?

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the Tanya's question: one who sees himself as a rasha will become sad and cannot serve Hashem with simcha, yet one who is always joyful may come to lightheadedness. He explains that 'like a rasha' means not being sure of oneself, and introduces the Gemara in Berachos on four kinds of people.

title.en: The Raya Mehemna on the four types

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives the simple meaning of tzaddik and rasha who fare well or badly, and then the Raya Mehemna in parshas Mishpatim: every person has a yetzer tov and a yetzer hara, and 'tzaddik vera lo' is a tzaddik who masters his evil, while 'rasha vetov lo' has a yetzer tov he does not obey.

title.en: Beinonim, Rabbah and Iyov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Berachos that tzaddikim are judged by the yetzer tov, reshaim by the yetzer hara and beinonim by both, Rabbah's saying that he is a beinoni and Abaye's reply. He then sets out the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when that is not decreed at birth, and how Rabbah, who never stopped learning, could err in calling himself a beinoni.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Mashgiach explains that the second week of consolation, Parshas Eikev, is a consolation of yiras Shamayim, and that Shabbos is a wellspring of yiras Shamayim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven weeks of consolation follow the middos. The first week is a consolation of chessed, with its double 'nachamu'. The second week, Parshas Eikev, is a consolation of yirah, fear of Heaven, and indeed the Torah's passage on yirah is read in Eikev. Just as the first week has the reading of Shema with its love, the second has yirah. He connects this to Shabbos, noting that the word Bereishis holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos': Shabbos gives yiras Shamayim. The consolation of this week is strengthening in yiras Shamayim, which many people greatly need; with today's yetzer hara in the street, guarding oneself is yiras Shamayim, and one should feel joy in it. The haftarah too speaks of those who fear Hashem. He calls Shabbos a wellspring of yiras Shamayim, and closes recalling Rav Shimon of Amshinov, a Jew of great yiras Shamayim.

en: The seven weeks of consolation follow the middos: the first is chessed, the second, Eikev, is yirah.
The consolation of Eikev is strengthening oneself in yiras Shamayim, which many people greatly need.
With today's yetzer hara in the street, guarding oneself is itself yiras Shamayim, and one should feel joy in it.
Shabbos is a wellspring of yiras Shamayim; on Shabbos one draws yiras Shamayim.

catalogTitle: A Song Depicting the Harmony of בריאה - the Essence of שבת (Intro. to מזמור שיר ליום השבת)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach introduces Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos as the song Shabbos itself sings: the harmony of all of creation, which will be seen in full on the day that is entirely Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the ten authors of Sefer Tehillim, all included in David HaMelech, the harp of seven strings that will have eight and then ten. He ties ten to the ten utterances of creation and explains that the tenth creation is menuchah, satisfaction, created on Shabbos and also found by a chassan and kallah. He then explains that Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos was David's portion in Torah, sung first by Adam HaRishon when Shabbos pleaded for him, and why Tehillim opens the way for tefillah in Pesukei D'zimra. Asking why the song of Shabbos never mentions Shabbos, he explains that the world was created with seven middos, seven notes; music is their harmonious arrangement. History is such a harmony, though a person sees only a dark patch, like a fly on a painting. Mizmor Shir sings of the day that is entirely Shabbos, when everyone will see the whole picture and have menuchah.

en: Sefer Tehillim has ten authors, matching the ten utterances of creation, yet all of it belongs to David HaMelech, the harp whose strings grow from seven to eight to ten.
The Mashgiach explains that menuchah, the satisfaction of lacking nothing, was itself a creation made on Shabbos, and the bond of chassan and kallah is that same creation.
Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos is David HaMelech's portion in Torah, which Adam HaRishon brought out first, with David's permission, after Shabbos pleaded for him.
Pesukei D'zimra, saying David's Tehillim before davening, cuts a path through the accusers, since David says his words together with the one who says them.
The world was created with seven middos, seven notes, and every event is one of them or a combination; music is their harmonious arrangement, not a random striking of keys.
Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos sings of the day that is entirely Shabbos, when the whole design of history will be seen and the world will have menuchah; the weekly Shabbos is a small taste of it.

title.en: Ten authors, one harp, ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the ten authors of Tehillim and says all of it is David HaMelech's, the harp of seven strings that will have eight with Moshiach and ten later. He links ten to the ten utterances of creation, and brings the Gemara that Bereishis itself is the first utterance containing all the others.

title.en: Menuchah: the creation of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bond of chassan and kallah is a creation called Shabbos, and brings Rashi that what the world lacked was menuchah, which was created on Shabbos. Menuchah means satisfaction; he then explains that Kabbalas Shabbos is made with Bo'i Kallah, and describes its three phases.

title.en: David's portion, sung first by Adam

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has his portion of chiddushim in Torah, which someone earlier may bring out before its time. Tehillim is David HaMelech's portion, and Adam HaRishon, saved from expulsion when Shabbos pleaded for him, sang Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos with David's permission.

title.en: Why Tehillim clears the way for tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says all yeshuos are in Sefer Tehillim, and explains that Pesukei D'zimra cuts away the accusers who block tefillos from rising. Since David says his words together with the one who says them, his name works like a royal stamp on a letter that the guards must let through.

title.en: The song Shabbos sings, and seven notes

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Levi'im's daily songs with Shabbos, where the day itself sings, since Shabbos completes the seven strings. He asks why this song never mentions Shabbos, and begins to answer: the world was created with seven middos, one per day, and every event and every sound is one of seven notes.

title.en: Music is harmony; so is history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that music is not random notes, like a cat on a piano, but notes arranged to match, which is why a chassan and kallah have music. The world is such a symphony: history fits together toward one purpose, and one who knows everything is for his good feels satisfied.

title.en: The fly on the painting and the great Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mizmor Shir speaks of the past, present and future of the world. Like a fly on a black patch of a masterpiece, people see only the dark part; when Moshiach comes, on the day that is entirely Shabbos, everyone will see the whole design and have menuchah, and the weekly Shabbos is a small reflection of it.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that all the mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus, attachment to Hashem, and that tefillah, said with the heart, with emunah and facing Yerushalayim, is the clearest form of that attachment.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar that the 613 mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus, being attached to Hashem. The soul is already holy; it came down so that the animal-like body should be purified through the mitzvos and share in that attachment. Tefillah is the true dveikus of the heart: the word itself means to attach, like tefillin bound tight, and Dovid HaMelech testifies that Hashem bends His ear to a Jew who prays. The Mashgiach urges davening with the meaning of the words, with a story about a poritz's mistake, and brings Rav Chaim Brisker that one must feel he stands before the King. Even a request for one's needs, a lower, not-for-its-own-sake prayer, fulfills emunah, as two Chassidic stories show. Finally he explains facing Yerushalayim in prayer: a person is where his thoughts are, as the Mishnah on techum Shabbos shows, and he closes with the days of Hod before Shavuos.

en: All 613 mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus with Hashem, which has many levels, from total absorption to simply feeling a closeness and a pleasure in it.
The soul is already holy; a person came into the world for the sake of the body, so that through the mitzvos it should be purified and itself attain dveikus.
Tefillah, the service of the heart, is the true dveikus; the word means attaching, as tefillin must be bound tight, and Hashem gives the one who prays His full attention.
One should daven with the meaning of the words and the awareness of standing before the King; one who keeps striving will find his heart opening sooner or later.
Asking Hashem for one's needs, even a small thing, is an act of emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments and the foundation of all mitzvos.
A Jew davens facing Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash, and since a person is where his thoughts are, in his tefillah he is truly there.

title.en: Mitzvos as counsel for dveikus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the 613 mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus, describes its levels, and explains that the soul came down so that the animal-like body should be purified through the mitzvos and also become attached to Hashem.

title.en: Tefillah is attachment; Hashem listens

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that davening, the service of the heart, is the true dveikus, derives tefillah from the root meaning to attach, as tefillin bound tight, and brings Dovid HaMelech and the Rosh Hashanah prayers that Hashem bends His ear and listens to a Jew who prays.

title.en: Davening with the heart; the poritz's mistake

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of davening with the heart, as in Ahavah Rabbah, brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that such davening would bring Moshiach, says that even mechanical understanding of the words is good, and tells of a poritz whose miscalculation went unnoticed because his mind was not busy, as some Jews' minds are, with accounts during Shemoneh Esrei.

title.en: Before the King; Torah for its own sake

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam and Rav Chaim Brisker that tefillah requires awareness of standing before the King, promises that persistent effort will open the heart, calls emunah the foundation of all mitzvos, and then lays out the levels of learning Torah for its own sake, adding that young bachurim must learn even not for its own sake.

title.en: Praying for needs is emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that praying for livelihood, children or health is tefillah not for its own sake, yet, as the Maharal and Rabbeinu Yonah say, it is a great thing, because it rests on the belief that Hashem can fulfill one's request, which is emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments.

title.en: Two tzaddikim ask for small things

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Dovid of Tolna delayed entering for the shofar blowing on Rosh Hashanah, ashamed to ask the great King for a roll, until he realized there is no one else to ask, and how a Chernobyler tzaddik asked Hashem that a household helper should not leave, explaining that one must ask Hashem for every small thing.

title.en: Facing Yerushalayim: where one's thought is

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara and Shlomo HaMelech's prayer that one davens toward Eretz Yisrael, Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies, explains why the Rishonim faced east and the Ba'al HaTanya's siddur southeast, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, proven from the Mishnah of one who sets his eyes on a tree for his Shabbos boundary.

title.en: In Yerushalayim at prayer; days of Hod

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that a Jew davening with kavanah toward Yerushalayim is there in his tefillah, then speaks of Pesach Sheni and the week of Hod leading to Lag BaOmer and Shavuos, bringing the Sfas Emes that the two loaves of Shavuos are Torah and tefillah, and closes with a blessing.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jewish emunah rests on the national revelation at Sinai and its unbroken tradition, and that our generation, the 'heel' of the body of Klal Yisroel, has emunah without feeling, yet its small avodah is especially precious to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam and the Kuzari: Jewish faith rests on the whole people standing at Sinai, something no other religion claims, and so the Torah will never be exchanged. Emunah, he says, is not grasped with the intellect, just as a picture is not heard and music is not seen. He then reads the Yismach Moshe's answer to a man troubled by doubts: a tradition received from six hundred thousand eyewitnesses cannot be a lie, since no parent could tell his child about an event nobody saw. Next comes the Bnei Yissaschar's question how the Rambam could write the Moreh Nevuchim if philosophical inquiry is forbidden, answered with the story of the Yismach Moshe and the Rambam's yiras shamayim. Finally the Mashgiach describes every generation, and all of history, as one body of Adam haRishon; ours is the heel, without feeling, yet our small avodah is precious, like the parrot in the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable.

en: Jewish emunah rests on the revelation at Sinai witnessed by the entire nation, which no other religion claims and which cannot be denied.
Hashem cannot be grasped with the intellect; another faculty is needed, just as the eye cannot hear music and the ear cannot see a picture.
Following the Yismach Moshe, a tradition from six hundred thousand eyewitnesses passed from parent to child cannot be a fabrication.
Every generation, and all of Jewish history together, forms one body of Adam haRishon, and each person has the choice to serve Hashem in the way of his place in it.
Ours is the generation of the heel, whose emunah is present but not felt, and therefore its small acts of avodah are especially precious to Hashem.

title.en: Emunah built on Sinai, not on the intellect

summary.en: Recalling the Rambam and the Kuzari, the Mashgiach explains that Jewish faith rests on a revelation the whole nation witnessed, unlike other religions, and cites the Rambam's principle that the Torah will never be exchanged. He lists ways to emunah and argues, with the parable of a picture and a symphony, that Hashem is not grasped by the intellect.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's answer to doubts

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Yismach Moshe's reply to a man plagued by doubts in emunah: the proof is not philosophy but the tradition received from six hundred thousand who saw, which no one could have invented and handed to his children. He adds that even other nations accept the miracles of Egypt, and lists the public miracles of the desert and of Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar's question on the Moreh Nevuchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's question: philosophical inquiry weighs both sides, so for a moment one entertains denial; how then could the Rambam write the Moreh Nevuchim? He answers that the Rambam was holy, and tells how the Yismach Moshe asked in Heaven for the Rambam's yiras shamayim and could not bear it.

title.en: The Rambam's katnus and answer before question

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates the Ba'al Shem Tov's comment that what the Yismach Moshe received was only the Rambam's mochin dekatnus, explains gadlus and katnus in tefillah, and concludes that the Rambam felt Hashem even while writing questions, writing for those who had strayed. From the order of Ein Kelokeinu he shows that a Jew must begin with the answer of emunah before asking.

title.en: Each generation as the body of Adam haRishon

summary.en: Bringing the Tanya and a Midrash, the Mashgiach explains that all souls hung from Adam haRishon, from head to toenails, so that each generation is a complete Adam haRishon: the head are the great Torah scholars, the heart the masters of tefillah, the hands the givers of tzedakah. Each person has the choice to use his gift for Hashem or for worldly things, illustrated with Reb Elchonon Wasserman and a wealthy man who gave to colleges.

title.en: Our generation is the heel without feeling

summary.en: The Mashgiach extends the image to all generations: the generation of the desert with Moshe Rabbeinu is the head, the generation of David and Shlomo the throat, and the last generation, ikvesa demeshicha, the heel. The heel has no feeling and stays dark even in the summer sun; so emunah today is present but unfelt, like a tooth pulled after a dentist's injection, unlike the Elul and tefillah of earlier generations.

title.en: The precious avodah of a low generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Reb Avraham of Ciechanow's joy at putting on tefillin with our small satisfaction, yet says our avodah is more precious in Heaven than that of earlier generations: holding back from interrupting learning or from idle talk is mesiras nefesh for us. He closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king who delights more in a talking parrot than in his wise ministers.

oneLiner.en: Opening the first chapter of Tanya for bachurim, the Mashgiach explains that every Jew has two souls, a holy one and one from kelipah, and that the lifelong war between them is the very purpose of coming into the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach introduces the Tanya's teaching, brought from the Arizal, that every Jew has two souls: one from holiness and one from kelipah, a word meaning a shell, like the shell of a nut. Foreign thoughts in davening do not mean something is wrong with a person; they come from the second soul, and the war against it is why souls that sang with the angels were sent down. Only rare tzaddikim finish the war. He then describes the four kelipos opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name through a rose among thorns and the walnut with its four shells, linking it to 'el ginas egoz yaradti' and to Yechezkel's vision, where the fourth, nogah, is light that passes through a barrier like a window shade. A Jew's body and yetzer come from nogah and can be elevated, chiefly by eating l'shem shamayim. Finally he reads the Tanya's text: Rabbi Chaim Vital's two souls, the sitra achra as the other side of a walled field, the animal soul in the blood, and the four elements.

en: Every Jew has two souls, one from holiness and one from kelipah, a shell that covers the edible fruit.
Foreign thoughts during davening come from the second soul and are no sign that something is wrong with the person.
Almost everyone is sent into the world to wage this war all his life; only rare tzaddikim finish it.
There are four kelipos opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name, like the four shells around the walnut's four sections.
The fourth kelipah, nogah, can be elevated; a Jew's body and yetzer come from it, while the three impure kelipos cannot be.
The animal soul resides in the blood, and from it come all bad traits, built of the four elements opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name.
